title: Yes means yes
hookLine: truthfulness in all speech, not just under oath

cards: "I swear, I'll be there at six." "Honestly, I loved it." "No, seriously, I'll pay you back."
Listen to how much extra packaging people wrap around ordinary sentences to make them believable. As if a plain sentence, left on its own, might not be true.

Jesus noticed the same habit in his own day, when people swore by heaven, by the earth, by Jerusalem, by their own heads, and quietly treated some oaths as more binding than others. His answer was short.

teach.b: It's in the Sermon on the Mount. After telling his listeners not to swear at all, Jesus says: "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil." Notice what that does.
If you need an oath to be believed, it suggests your ordinary words are a lower grade of truth.

teach.h: ONE KIND OF SPEECH, NOT TWO.
teach.b: Swearing creates two kinds of speech: the sworn kind you must keep, and the everyday kind you can bend. Jesus folds them back into one. Every word is meant to be the sworn kind.
James, writing to early Christians, repeats it almost word for word: "let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay." Christians have applied this in different ways.
Quakers, Mennonites and some other churches take it literally and decline to swear oaths, even in court; they make a solemn affirmation instead.

teach.h: NO OATHS, OR NO CARELESS ONES.
teach.b: Other churches read Jesus as forbidding careless and manipulative oaths, not every oath. They point out that Paul calls God as his witness in his letters, and they allow oaths in court and at ordination.

Both sides agree on the heart of it: a person whose plain word can be trusted without extra packaging. Yesterday's warning was about not making the little ones stumble. This one is about not making anyone guess.
A yes that means yes. A no that means no.
And no secret third option hidden behind the words.

how: Quakers, Mennonites and some other Christians decline to swear oaths and make a solemn affirmation in court instead; other churches permit oaths for solemn occasions while teaching that all ordinary speech should be truthful.

o: always agree when someone asks you for help
always do whatever a friend asks you to do
let a plain yes or no be as true as an oath

games.q: about plain speech — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus only cared about telling the truth under oath
he folds sworn and ordinary speech into one: every yes should be a real yes.
some Christians decline to swear even in court
Quakers, Mennonites and some others make a solemn affirmation instead.
all churches read this as forbidding every oath
some do; others read it as forbidding careless oaths, and point to Paul calling God as his witness.

games.q: you're a Quaker called as a witness. the clerk holds out a Bible and asks you to swear. what do you do?
o: make a solemn affirmation instead, and tell the truth.
games.why: Quakers take "swear not at all" literally and affirm instead, where the court allows it. the point isn't to avoid the truth; it's that every word should already be true.

practice: Think of one thing you've said you would do that's still hanging, a call you promised, a favor, something you told a kid, and hold it plainly: no excuses, no reasons, just the yes you gave.
Then notice how often your sentences reach for honestly or I swear, and whether they could stand on their own. If you pray, you can offer your words to God.

wordCard.voice: Yes means yes. Jesus's teaching in Matthew 5: let your yea be yea and your nay, nay, so that every plain word is as true as an oath.

orig.note: Greek, Matthew 5:37: yes, yes; no, no.

carryVoice: Your line: plain truth. A plain yes, on its own, can be enough. See you soon.
